CMADT: Sebokeng paediatric ER

By: Laura Byrne | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust is once again stepping in to provide for our most vulnerable, with a paediatric trauma unit at Sebokeng Hospital.

Unique Selling Point:
It's a story about consistency in our mission, and refusing to compromise on the dream of improving state healthcare facilities for children in desperate need. The Trust has worked with Sebokeng Hospital for over a decade, providing an Infant High Care Ward and a Paediatric Lower High Care Ward. Now, the Trust is stepping in to provide a first-of-its-kind trauma facility to Sebokeng's children.


Summary:
When a child faces an emergency such as an accident or a burn injury, they are rushed to the trauma unit of the nearest hospital - along with every adult who has been in a barfight, a shoot-out, or a car accident. In the vast majority of South Africa's emergency departments, there is no distinction between adult and child patients - much to the children's detriment. Children exhibit shock and distress differently, requiring different triage techniques and knowledge. Their tiny bodies need to be treated with smaller instruments and special techniques. And they can be traumatised, their situations worsened, by the violence they are exposed to in the emergency department. At Sebokeng, Head of Paediatrics Dr Teletsane is well aware of this, which is why he has given up his office to set aside space for the children who arrive at the hospital's trauma unit, and the staff who must treat them. But an office is no paediatric ward. The hospital desperately needs dedicated and specialised facilities for paediatric emergencies - which is where the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has stepped in.

Further information:
Our story will take place in two halves: we will spend a day between Dr Teletsane's makeshift paediatric trauma unit and the adult emergency department where children must return after being triaged, to be treated for broken bones and other emergencies. We will hear about Dr Teletsane's determination to provide a space for children to be safely treated by specialised staff, and about the particular needs of a paediatric trauma unit.
We will then spend a day on the site of the brand new paediatric emergency department that is under construction thanks to the Trust and its partners and donors. We will conduct a site visit with the specialised team overseeing the build, and hear what exactly goes into the design and building of a hospital.

We will also reference the broader work of the Trust within the theme of consistency and follow-through, highlighting the recently completed Paediatric Outpatient Burns Unit at Ngwelezana Hospital in KZN.

Press Release:


When a child is in an accident or suffers a burn injury, they are rushed to the emergency unit of the nearest hospital – along with every adult in need of urgent care. In most South African casualty wards, there is no distinction between adult and child patients, much to the children’s detriment. They need specialised triage techniques and knowledge, and adult equipment is not designed for tiny bodies. At Sebokeng Regional Hospital, the situation for young patients has become dire. Now the Carte Blanche Making a Different Trust has stepped in. The Trust undertakes special projects for paediatric units in state hospitals. Having recently completed a Paediatric Burns Outpatient Department at Ngwelezana Hospital in KwaZulu Natal, the MAD Trust is creating a first-of-its-kind children’s trauma facility in its third project at Sebokeng Hospital.

Script:


UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: Welcome to what used to be my office…
Erin Bates: Your desk is still there but we’re busy saving a baby’s life.
VOICEOVER: It’s a space more suited to paperwork than complex medical treatment: an office converted to a makeshift ER. But it’s challenges like these that the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust turns into opportunities to transform children’s lives.
LINK: Your child is injured. You rush her to emergency – along with every adult who’s been in a bar fight, a shoot-out, or a car crash. In most South African hospitals, there’s little distinction between child and adult emergencies, which means everyone is treated on the same first-come, first-served basis.
UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: We don’t have an ICU. We should get a child, stabilise the child, and then look for space in a tertiary centre where they have ICU.
VOICEOVER: Dr Thapehlo Theletsane is head of paediatrics at Sebokeng Regional Hospital, which serves the 1.3 million people of Sedibeng District.
UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: Because the ICUs are almost always full, we are forced to be stuck with a child where we have to do everything.
VOICEOVER: In the last decade, the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has built two paediatric high-care wards at Sebokeng. But they’re operating beyond capacity.
UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: This facility is affording us the ability to continue with intensive care…
Erin Bates: But only just, right. You need more.
Dr Theletsane: Ja. We need more. Beautiful as it is, it's not enough to meet the needs of the children of Sedibeng.
VOICEOVER: Children need special expertise and treatment. Medics trained in adult emergencies might not recognise a child in severe distress. The equipment is not designed for tiny bodies… and babies can be exposed to additional risks in casualty, like infection.
UPSOUND: Sister Namane: that's when we came up with the concept of having our own paediatric consultation room.
VOICEOVER: Sister Andronica Namane is operational manager of the paediatric Lower High Care facility.
UPSOUND: Sister Namane: That's when Dr Theletsane's room came into place, whereby it’s our temporary paediatric casualty at the moment.
VOICEOVER: Here, children are treated with other children by specialist doctors and nurses.
UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: Within 30 minutes of a child arriving here, would have been seen by a trained nurse in paediatrics and a trained doctor in paediatrics.
VOICEOVER: But ingenuity and passion alone can’t transform this cramped space into a suitable treatment area.
UPSOUND: Sister Namane: We don't have a waiting area. So we’re basically using the passage as a waiting area. Number two, the consultation room is supposed to have oxygen, medical points, enough space between the doctor and the patients and the parent. If we have an emergency, suddenly we have to evacuate everybody. Sometimes we don't have anywhere to take them, which is a big challenge for us.
LINK: This one-month-old baby is receiving critical medical care in a head of department’s office. But with the help of the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust, all of this will change for babies just like little Palesa in time to come.
VOICEOVER: Since 2008, the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has built over 22 dedicated paediatric facilities in state hospitals around South Africa. Its most recent triumph is a paediatric outpatient burns unit at Ngwelezana Hospital in KwaZulu Natal, completed last year with a principal capital donation from South32’s Hillside Aluminium and the ongoing support of our professional partners and material donors. Here, children with burns injuries now receive the long-term treatment they need at a specialist facility.
At Sebokeng, an even more ambitious project is quickly taking shape with the support of the same partners.
LINK: If you think this is any old building site, think again. This is the makings of a highly specialised centre. We’re talking a children’s casualty unit.
UPSOUND: Braam van der Hoven: On the design we incorporate those skylights into the pattern…
VOICEOVER: Architect Braam van der Hoven is the project’s lead designer, and has worked with the Trust for over a decade.
UPSOUND: Erin Bates: It is pro bono work, it's time and money and your skill. What drives you?
Braam van der Hoven: Well children is important. It's the future and it's needed. So it's a way of giving back.
VOICEOVER: This site, nestled tightly between the hospital’s existing buildings, will soon be transformed into a child-friendly space filled with natural light.
UPSOUND: Braam van der Hoven: It's important to lay out the perfect solution, because a unit like this is always under a compromise. In this instance, it's space. So you lay out the technical requirements. And from there you need to prioritize what is important.
VOICEOVER: The deceptively simple layout has been meticulously planned down to the very last centimetre.
UPSOUND: Constance Bajomo: It's important to understand the flow of the unit. [...] As the parent come in with the sick child, there is a nurse station there. If there's a child who is in trouble, you’ll see them as they come in.
VOICEOVER: Health facilities planner Constance Bajomo developed the project’s clinical brief, which details how every space in the building will be used.
UPSOUND: Constance Bajomo: This is more like your ICU. So if this child needs life support, they will be able to manage the child there. The next one is your counselling room. This is our treatment area… It's open because it needs to be visible to the nurse station which will be in the middle here.
VOICEOVER: The new unit is designed to meet all the needs of a family in a medical emergency - from the resuscitation bays tucked out of sight for privacy, to the play area for siblings.
UPSOUND: Constance Bajomo: This is a very interesting project for me and the team because we've never developed a specific paediatric emergency unit.
VOICEOVER: But building a new unit and integrating it with the existing hospital is not an easy process.
LINK: With a build like this, you have to dig deep - not only figuratively, but in this case, literally!
VOICEOVER: Before building could begin, one thousand cubic metres of soil had to be excavated and replaced.
UPSOUND: Johan du Plessis: We couldn't do just a normal strip foundations due to the soil not being able to carry the loads from the building. So we needed to design a raft foundation.
VOICEOVER: Johan du Plessis is the project’s structural technician.
UPSOUND: Erin Bates: So for us who aren't builders, what is a raft foundation?
Johan du Plessis: So a raft foundation is what it says. It's floating on top of the soil. It spreads the loads quite a lot more. So with the raft, the entire building will move on top of it.
UPSOUND: Braam van der Hoven: From now on, the most technically difficult part will be tying into the existing services and also linking into the walkways and the adjoining buildings.
VOICEOVER: But the way forward is clear and bright. The hospital has already received a budget to co-staff the new unit, which will be completed by July.
UPSOUND: Erin Bates: What will be, do you think, the most powerful moment for you?
Braam van der Hoven: I think to see the first patients being served, that's the proudest moment.
VOICEOVER: As for Dr Theletsane and his staff, the new centre simply can’t come quickly enough.
UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: We're not only just dealing with children, this child comes from a family, and this family is coming from a community. And I think in the longer term, the overall health status of children in this district will be improved.
UPSOUND: Sister Namane: An environment that will say, I'm child friendly, I'm family friendly, we care for you. That place will be perfecto for us.

PROMOS

PROMO 1
VOICEOVER: The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has built two paediatric high-care wards at Sebokeng District Hospital…. But they’re operating beyond capacity.
UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: Beautiful as it is, it's not good enough to meet the needs of the children of Sedibeng.
VOICEOVER: So the Trust has taken on an even more ambitious project: a children’s casualty unit.

PROMO 2
LINK: This is the story about refusing to compromise on the dream of making a difference for children in desperate need.
UPSOUND: Sister Namane: An environment that will say, I'm child friendly, I’m family friendly, we care for you.
VOICEOVER: Here at Sebokeng Hospital, the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust is building a first-of-its-kind emergency facility.

PROMO 3
UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: This new unit will significantly reduce the mortality…
VOICEOVER: At Sebokeng District Hospital, an ambitious project is taking shape, thanks to the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust.
UPSOUND: Braam van der Hoven: We believe in what the trust believes. Children is important. It's the future and it's needed.

PROMO 4
VOICEOVER: A child in a medical emergency needs a specialised approach that’s unavailable in many South African casualty units.
UPSOUND: Dr Theletsane: You don't want to be exposing them to terrible things like stab wounds.
VOICEOVER: But Sebokeng Regional Hospital will soon have its very own dedicated paediatric emergency centre, thanks to the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust is once again stepping in to provide for our most vulnerable, with a paediatric trauma unit at Sebokeng Hospital.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It's a story about consistency in our mission, and refusing to compromise on the dream of improving state healthcare facilities for children in desperate need. The Trust has worked with Sebokeng Hospital for over a decade, providing an Infant High Care Ward and a Paediatric Lower High Care Ward. Now, the Trust is stepping in to provide a first-of-its-kind trauma facility to Sebokeng's children.
metadata.Summary: When a child faces an emergency such as an accident or a burn injury, they are rushed to the trauma unit of the nearest hospital - along with every adult who has been in a barfight, a shoot-out, or a car accident. In the vast majority of South Africa's emergency departments, there is no distinction between adult and child patients - much to the children's detriment. Children exhibit shock and distress differently, requiring different triage techniques and knowledge. Their tiny bodies need to be treated with smaller instruments and special techniques. And they can be traumatised, their situations worsened, by the violence they are exposed to in the emergency department. At Sebokeng, Head of Paediatrics Dr Teletsane is well aware of this, which is why he has given up his office to set aside space for the children who arrive at the hospital's trauma unit, and the staff who must treat them. But an office is no paediatric ward. The hospital desperately needs dedicated and specialised facilities for paediatric emergencies - which is where the Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust has stepped in.
metadata.Further information: Our story will take place in two halves: we will spend a day between Dr Teletsane's makeshift paediatric trauma unit and the adult emergency department where children must return after being triaged, to be treated for broken bones and other emergencies. We will hear about Dr Teletsane's determination to provide a space for children to be safely treated by specialised staff, and about the particular needs of a paediatric trauma unit. We will then spend a day on the site of the brand new paediatric emergency department that is under construction thanks to the Trust and its partners and donors. We will conduct a site visit with the specialised team overseeing the build, and hear what exactly goes into the design and building of a hospital. We will also reference the broader work of the Trust within the theme of consistency and follow-through, highlighting the recently completed Paediatric Outpatient Burns Unit at Ngwelezana Hospital in KZN.
